set.stem: A 16-year-old boy has a 6-month history of worsening breathlessness and a daily productive cough yielding about a cupful of sputum. He had severe measles in childhood and has smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 2 years. He looks unwell, with mild dyspnoea, early finger clubbing and bilateral coarse crackles over the lower zones; cardiac examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Copious daily purulent sputum, coarse basal crackles and clubbing in a young patient with severe childhood measles is post-infective bronchiectasis. Two years of light smoking cannot cause chronic bronchitis, which also does not cause clubbing; asthma gives variable wheeze without large sputum volumes, tuberculosis favours the upper zones with constitutional symptoms, and interstitial lung disease causes a dry cough with fine crackles. High-resolution CT confirms the diagnosis.

set.stem: A 16-year-old boy has a daily productive cough yielding about a cupful of purulent sputum, bilateral coarse basal crackles and early finger clubbing. He had severe measles in early childhood and has no occupational exposures. Which underlying cause of his condition is most likely?
set.explanation: Severe childhood lower respiratory infections, especially measles, whooping cough and tuberculosis, damage the bronchial wall's elastic and muscular tissue; the damaged airways dilate, clear mucus poorly and enter a vicious cycle of infection and inflammation, producing bronchiectasis. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency mainly causes basal emphysema in adults, asbestos exposure causes pleural plaques and asbestosis decades later in workers, and pulmonary hypertension and sarcoidosis do not cause copious purulent sputum.

why: Source key (occupational asbestos exposure) was wrong; post-measles damage is the cause. Stem rewritten to stand alone

set.stem: Apart from post-infective damage (e.g. after measles or whooping cough), which of the following is a recognised cause of bronchiectasis in young patients?
set.explanation: Cystic fibrosis causes thick, dehydrated airway mucus from defective CFTR chloride transport, leading to chronic infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas) and widespread upper-lobe bronchiectasis from childhood. Other causes to look for in the young are primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunoglobulin deficiency and ABPA. Pulmonary embolism, mitral stenosis, pneumothorax and coarctation do not damage the bronchial wall.

set.explanation: Haemoptysis is common in bronchiectasis because chronic inflammation enlarges and multiplies the bronchial arteries (systemic pressure), which bleed easily; it ranges from streaks to massive bleeding needing bronchial artery embolisation. Other complications are recurrent infective exacerbations, pneumonia, empyema, cor pulmonale in advanced disease and, rarely, amyloidosis. Pneumothorax is uncommon except in cystic fibrosis, and tamponade and aortic dissection are unrelated.

set.explanation: On HRCT a dilated bronchus seen end-on next to its smaller accompanying pulmonary artery looks like a signet ring, and a bronchoarterial ratio above 1 is the key diagnostic sign of bronchiectasis, together with lack of tapering and bronchi visible within 1 cm of the pleura. Honeycombing indicates fibrotic ILD such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, ground-glass opacity is non-specific alveolitis or oedema, tree-in-bud reflects small-airway infection (it may accompany bronchiectasis but is not specific), and consolidation means airspace filling.

set.explanation: In bronchiectasis, damaged dilated airways with impaired mucociliary clearance become chronically colonised (Haemophilus, Pseudomonas); the neutrophilic inflammation causes mucus hypersecretion and pus, producing large daily volumes of purulent sputum. This is why airway clearance physiotherapy is the cornerstone of treatment. Heart failure produces frothy pink sputum, bronchorrhoea from tumours is rare and watery, and allergic hypersecretion gives small volumes of mucoid sputum.

set.stem: Which of the following is NOT a measure for the prevention and control of tuberculosis?
set.explanation: Tuberculosis is controlled by rapid case-finding and complete treatment of infectious cases (directly observed therapy prevents default and drug resistance), respiratory isolation of smear-positive patients for the first 2 weeks of treatment, contact tracing with preventive therapy (e.g. 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid or 6 months of isoniazid) for latent infection, and BCG vaccination of infants in high-prevalence areas. Pneumococcal vaccination protects against Streptococcus pneumoniae and has no effect on tuberculosis.

set.stem: Regarding the adverse effects of antituberculous drugs, which statement is true?
options: Asymptomatic rises in transaminases are common but serious liver damage is rare
Ethambutol causes red-orange discoloration of urine
set.explanation: Mild asymptomatic transaminase rises are common in the first weeks of treatment and usually settle, whereas clinical hepatitis is uncommon; LFTs are checked at baseline and repeated if symptoms or risk factors. Peripheral neuropathy is caused by isoniazid (prevented with pyridoxine), red-orange urine and tears by rifampicin, and optic neuritis by ethambutol (check visual acuity and colour vision). Streptomycin is ototoxic to the fetus and is avoided in pregnancy.

set.stem: A 34-year-old woman who initially complained of nasal obstruction develops cough, haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. Her chest X-ray shows multiple nodular masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Upper airway disease (nasal obstruction, crusting, epistaxis, sinusitis) followed by haemoptysis and multiple, often cavitating lung nodules is granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a necrotising vasculitis with c-ANCA (PR3) positivity that may also cause glomerulonephritis. EGPA occurs in asthmatics with eosinophilia, Goodpasture syndrome causes alveolar haemorrhage and nephritis without nasal disease or nodules, and multiple masses in a young woman with nasal symptoms are unlikely to be lung cancer.

set.stem: Which of the following findings best suggests active pulmonary tuberculosis?
set.explanation: Cavitation reflects liquefied caseous necrosis discharging into a bronchus and indicates active, usually smear-positive and infectious, post-primary tuberculosis. A raised ESR is non-specific, fibrosis and calcified hilar nodes are signs of old healed disease, and a positive tuberculin test shows only past sensitisation (latent infection or BCG). Sputum AFB smear and culture must still confirm the diagnosis.

set.stem: A 30-year-old woman has high continuous fever, rigors, breathlessness and a cough productive of rusty sputum. Pneumococcal lobar pneumonia is suspected. If her sputum is sent for Gram stain, which finding is expected?
set.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus, often capsulated; rusty sputum reflects red cells in the alveolar exudate. Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci, Gram-negative rods suggest Klebsiella, Pseudomonas or Haemophilus (small coccobacilli), and acid-fast bacilli indicate mycobacteria. BTS guidance advises sputum and blood cultures plus pneumococcal urinary antigen in moderate or high-severity pneumonia.

set.stem: What is the typical chest X-ray finding in lobar pneumonia?
set.explanation: Lobar pneumonia fills the alveoli of a lobe with exudate, producing homogeneous consolidation limited by the fissures, often with air bronchograms and a silhouette sign against the adjacent heart border or diaphragm. Diffuse interstitial shadowing suggests atypical or viral pneumonia or ILD, hyperlucency suggests emphysema or pneumothorax, cavities suggest abscess or tuberculosis, and miliary nodules suggest haematogenous tuberculosis. Radiological resolution lags behind clinical recovery by up to 6 weeks.

set.stem: A 45-year-old man returns from a holiday in Spain with a week of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, cough and confusion. His chest X-ray is shown. What abnormality is seen?
set.explanation: The film shows extensive airspace opacification of the left mid and lower zones with air bronchograms and preserved lung volume, i.e. consolidation from pneumonia. A large effusion would give a homogeneous opacity with a meniscus and mediastinal shift away, an empyema a D-shaped pleural-based opacity, a carcinoma a mass or collapse, and a pulmonary infarct a small wedge-shaped pleural-based shadow. The travel history, confusion and severity should raise suspicion of Legionella.

set.stem: A 45-year-old man returns from a hotel holiday in Spain with a week of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, cough and new confusion (abbreviated mental test score 6/10). T 39.4°C, RR 26/min, BP 118/74 mmHg. Serum urea 9.8 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L. The chest X-ray shows extensive left-sided consolidation. What is his CURB-65 score?
set.explanation: He scores 1 for new confusion and 1 for urea above 7 mmol/L, giving a CURB-65 score of 2; respiratory rate is below 30/min, systolic BP is not below 90 mmHg nor diastolic 60 mmHg or less, and he is under 65. A score of 2 is moderate severity (30-day mortality about 9%), so BTS guidance advises hospital treatment with amoxicillin plus clarithromycin. Clinical judgement still matters: extensive consolidation and hyponatraemia after hotel travel suggest Legionella, and urinary antigen should be sent.

set.stem: A 45-year-old man returns from a hotel holiday in Spain with a week of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, dry cough, diarrhoea and new confusion. Sodium 126 mmol/L, ALT 140 U/L, CK raised; the chest X-ray shows extensive left-sided consolidation. Which is the most likely causative organism?
set.explanation: Legionella pneumophila is acquired by inhaling aerosols from contaminated water systems (hotel air-conditioning, showers, cooling towers); it causes severe pneumonia with confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, deranged liver tests, raised CK and lymphopenia. Diagnosis is by urinary antigen (serogroup 1) and sputum PCR or culture, and treatment is with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia pneumoniae cause milder illness in younger people, Haemophilus affects COPD patients, and pneumococcus lacks the travel and biochemical clues.

why: Fragment of a split question rebuilt to stand alone; source key (Chlamydia pneumoniae) contradicted its own explanation (Legionella)

set.stem: A 38-year-old man presents with cough productive of blood-streaked sputum, fever and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He also has cold sores. His chest X-ray is shown. What does it show?
set.explanation: There is patchy airspace opacification at the left base with loss of definition of the left hemidiaphragm, i.e. left basal (lower-lobe) consolidation; with rusty sputum, pleurisy and herpes labialis this is typical pneumococcal pneumonia. A pneumothorax would show a visible pleural edge without lung markings, collapse would show volume loss with shift of fissures or mediastinum, an effusion a meniscus, and reticulonodular shadowing a diffuse interstitial pattern.
